description: South Korea's largest park, with one of the steepest wooden coasters in the world and a tulip festival that draws as many people as the rides.

title: Skate the indoor rink at Lotte World
description: The largest indoor theme park on earth, with an outdoor island section on a lake, connected by monorail and open whatever the weather does.

title: Spend a day at Universal Studios Singapore
description: Compact enough to do properly in one day, on a resort island reached by cable car, monorail or a boardwalk you can simply walk across.

title: Ride Formula Rossa at Ferrari World
description: The fastest roller coaster in the world at 240km/h, which is quick enough that riders are issued safety goggles before boarding.

title: Ride the Wild Mouse at Luna Park Sydney
description: Under the Harbour Bridge since 1935, behind a giant grinning face. The 1959 Wild Mouse is one of the last of its kind still running anywhere.

title: Kayak beneath the cliffs at Pictured Rocks
description: 60m sandstone cliffs on Lake Superior, streaked blue, orange and green by mineral seepage. The lake is cold enough to be genuinely dangerous.

title: Run down the dune climb at Sleeping Bear
description: A 137m sand bluff above Lake Michigan. Going down takes two minutes; coming back up takes most people close to an hour.

title: Cycle around car-free Mackinac Island
description: Motor vehicles have been banned since 1898, so everything moves by horse, bicycle or foot. The shore road is a flat 13km loop.

title: Portage a canoe through the Boundary Waters
description: More than 1,000 lakes linked by portage trails, with motors banned across most of it. You carry the canoe over your head between the water.

title: Walk into the Apostle Islands ice caves
description: Sea caves hung with icicles, reachable on foot only when the lake freezes solid enough - which has happened just a handful of times this century.

title: Take the architecture cruise on the Chicago River
description: The city rebuilt after the 1871 fire and invented the skyscraper doing it. The river was also reversed in 1900 so it flows away from the lake.

title: See your reflection in Cloud Gate
description: Anish Kapoor's 110-tonne stainless steel bean, welded from 168 plates with every seam polished away.

title: Ride the tram to the top of the Gateway Arch
description: 192m of stainless steel catenary curve, ascended in a tram of tilting five-person pods designed in two weeks in 1960.

title: See the exhibits at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
place: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
description: In Cleveland because a DJ here popularised the term in the early 1950s. I M Pei designed the glass pyramid on the lakefront.

title: Go underground at Mammoth Cave
description: Over 685km mapped and still growing - by a wide margin the longest cave system known anywhere, and more than twice the next longest.

title: Follow the Kentucky Bourbon Trail
description: Around 95% of the world's bourbon is made in Kentucky, ageing in charred new oak in warehouses you can walk through and smell from the road.

title: Watch the synchronous fireflies in the Smokies
description: For about two weeks each June, one firefly species here flashes in unison. Access is by lottery, and it is worth entering.

title: Hear a songwriter round in Nashville
description: Broadway is the loud version; the Bluebird Cafe and the writers' rounds are where the songs actually get made, in rooms of ninety people.

title: Stand in the studio where Elvis recorded at Sun
description: A single small room where Elvis, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins and Jerry Lee Lewis all recorded. Still a working studio at night.

title: Visit the National Civil Rights Museum at the Lorraine Motel
description: Built around the balcony where Martin Luther King Jr was killed in 1968. Room 306 is preserved exactly as it was that afternoon.

title: Follow the brass bands down Frenchmen Street
description: Where locals go when tourists go to Bourbon Street - live jazz in a dozen rooms within three blocks, most nights of the year.

title: Take a boat into the Atchafalaya swamp
description: The largest wetland and swamp in the US - bald cypress hung with Spanish moss, alligators, and a way of life built entirely on the water.

title: Walk the squares of Savannah
description: Laid out in 1733 around 24 public squares, 22 of which survive, under live oaks hung with Spanish moss.

title: See the wild horses on Cumberland Island
description: A barrier island reachable only by ferry, with feral horses on the dunes and the ruins of a Carnegie mansion in the maritime forest.

title: Paddle the mangroves in the Everglades
description: A river 100km wide and 15cm deep, and the only place where alligators and crocodiles share territory. Go in the dry season for the wildlife.

title: Drive the Overseas Highway to Key West
description: 180km over 42 bridges to the southernmost point in the continental US, built on the piers of Flagler's railway destroyed by a hurricane in 1935.

title: Snorkel the fort moat at Dry Tortugas
description: 113km west of Key West by ferry or seaplane - a vast unfinished brick fort on a sand key, with coral growing along the moat wall.

title: Watch a rocket launch from the Space Coast
description: Launch cadence is now high enough that a week here will usually catch one. The Saturn V hanging in the visitor complex is a real one.

title: Snorkel with manatees at Crystal River
description: The only place in the US where supervised in-water encounters with manatees are legal - they gather in the 22C springs when the gulf turns cold.

title: Walk the Battery in Charleston
description: Antebellum houses along the seawall, and the harbour where the Civil War began at Fort Sumter in 1861.

title: Drive the Blue Ridge Parkway in autumn
description: 755km of ridge road with no commercial traffic and a 72km/h limit. The colour moves down the mountain about 30m a day through October.

title: Climb the Cape Hatteras lighthouse
description: 257 steps up the tallest brick lighthouse in the US, on a barrier island so mobile the whole structure was moved 880m inland in 1999.

title: Walk the catwalk under the New River Gorge Bridge
description: A 24-inch catwalk 260m above the river, under the bridge deck. One day each October it is legal to BASE jump off the top.

title: Drive Skyline Drive through Shenandoah
description: 170km along the Blue Ridge crest with 75 overlooks. One of the few national parks where dogs are allowed on almost every trail.

title: Watch the pony swim at Chincoteague
description: Feral ponies swim the channel between islands each July, herded by the volunteer fire brigade who have run it since 1925.

title: Spend a day in the Smithsonian museums
description: Nineteen museums, all free, including Air and Space and the National Museum of African American History and Culture - the last needs timed passes.

title: Walk the memorials on the National Mall after dark
description: Lincoln, Vietnam and Korea are all open 24 hours and lit at night, when they are far quieter and considerably more affecting.

title: See the cherry blossom at the Tidal Basin
description: 3,000 trees given by Tokyo in 1912. Peak bloom lasts a few days and the date is forecast each year - it has been trending earlier for decades.

title: Tour Fallingwater
description: Frank Lloyd Wright cantilevered a house directly over a waterfall in 1935. Tours must be booked and sell out weeks ahead in autumn.

title: See the Liberty Bell and Independence Hall
description: Both the Declaration and the Constitution were debated in the same room. Free timed tickets, and the queue moves faster than it looks.

title: Walk Pickett's Charge at Gettysburg
description: Crossing the mile of open field the Confederate infantry walked into artillery fire in 1863 tells you more than any museum can.

title: Walk the High Line end to end
description: A disused elevated freight line turned 2.3km linear park through Manhattan's west side. Free, and dogs are not permitted.

title: Cross the Brooklyn Bridge on foot at dawn
description: The first steel-wire suspension bridge, opened 1883. Walk Brooklyn to Manhattan at first light and you will have the promenade to yourself.

title: Spend an afternoon in the Met
description: Two million works across 5,000 years, including an entire Egyptian temple moved stone by stone. Pick two wings and accept you will miss the rest.

title: Eat your way through a New York deli
description: Pastrami cured for weeks and steamed for hours, in rooms that have not been redecorated since the 1950s and are better for it.

title: Count the waterfalls at Watkins Glen
description: Nineteen waterfalls in three kilometres, on a stone path cut into the gorge that goes behind, under and over the water.

title: See all three falls at Letchworth
description: Called the Grand Canyon of the East - a 27km gorge with 180m walls and three major waterfalls, and hot air balloons over it in autumn.

title: Walk the Freedom Trail in Boston
description: 4km of red brick line through sixteen sites, from Boston Common to the Bunker Hill Monument, taking in most of the American Revolution.

title: Cycle the Cape Cod Rail Trail
description: 40km of flat former railway through pitch pine and cranberry bog, with the Atlantic dunes of the National Seashore at the far end.

title: See the first sunrise in the US from Cadillac Mountain
description: From October to March this is the first place in the continental US to catch the sun. Acadia is unusually dog-friendly for a national park.

title: Climb the iron rungs of the Beehive Trail
description: Iron rungs and narrow ledges bolted to a granite cliff, climbed in one direction only. Short, and not for anyone uneasy about exposure.

title: Eat a lobster roll on a working wharf
description: Maine lands most of the country's lobster. The argument over warm butter versus cold mayonnaise is genuine and locals hold firm views.

title: Drive the Kancamagus Highway in October
description: 55km through the White Mountain National Forest with no petrol, no shops and no phone signal - just sugar maples doing their thing.

title: Ride the cog railway up Mount Washington
description: The world's first mountain-climbing cog railway, running since 1869, up a summit that held the world land wind speed record at 372km/h for sixty years.

title: Chase the autumn colour through Vermont
description: Sugar maples turn earliest and brightest here, and the state runs a foliage tracker because the peak moves south about 50km a week.

title: Walk the Newport Cliff Walk past the mansions
description: 5.6km between Gilded Age summer houses and the Atlantic, with public access preserved by colonial-era shoreline rights the owners have fought for a century.

title: Cross the Edmund Pettus Bridge at Selma
description: Where marchers were beaten on Bloody Sunday in 1965, an event that moved the Voting Rights Act through Congress within months.

title: Drive the Natchez Trace Parkway
description: 715km following a path used for thousands of years, with no commercial traffic and sections of the original sunken trace you can walk.

title: Dig for diamonds at Crater of Diamonds
description: The only diamond-bearing site in the world open to the public where you keep what you find. Several hundred are found each year, most of them small.

title: Sit with the lynching memorial in Montgomery
place: National Memorial for Peace and Justice
description: Eight hundred hanging steel columns, one for each county where a lynching took place, each carrying names. Allow the whole afternoon and expect it to be hard.

title: Swim off the quartz sand at Gulf State Park
description: Sand ground down from Appalachian quartz, so it stays cool underfoot in August, with 45km of trail behind the dunes.

title: Stand under a Saturn V at the Rocket Center
description: The largest collection of rockets anywhere, including a Saturn V lying on its side that is longer than a football pitch.

title: Bathe in a Hot Springs bathhouse
description: Forty-seven springs at 62 degrees plumbed into Edwardian bathhouses in the middle of town. The Buckstaff still runs the old way.

title: Paddle the Buffalo National River
description: The first national river in the country, protected undammed in 1972, beneath limestone bluffs 150 metres above the water.

title: Paddle into the Okefenokee at dawn
description: A peat bog the size of a county holding perhaps ten thousand alligators, with water stained black by tannin and overnight platforms out in it.

title: Walk the Atlanta BeltLine Eastside Trail
description: A disused rail loop being turned into 35km of park and path around the city. The Eastside stretch is finished, free and always busy.

title: Walk out onto the Ledge at Skydeck
description: Glass boxes cantilevered 412 metres up with nothing under your feet but Wacker Drive.

title: Follow what is left of Route 66 through Illinois
description: The original alignment still runs in pieces beside the interstate, through diners and neon that survived being bypassed in 1977.

title: Climb or walk the arches of Red River Gorge
description: More than a hundred natural sandstone arches, and some of the best sport climbing in the country on the same rock.

title: Stand at the Churchill Downs finish line
description: The Derby has run on the first Saturday in May since 1875. Outside race week the track and museum are quiet and cheap.

title: See the mill buildings full of art at MASS MoCA
description: Twenty-six former factory buildings in North Adams, holding art too big for a normal gallery, including a Sol LeWitt wall drawing retrospective on for decades.

title: Watch whales on Stellwagen Bank
description: A submerged sandbank that concentrates sand lance, and with them humpbacks that feed by blowing nets of bubbles.

title: Drive the North Shore to Grand Marais
description: A hundred and fifty miles along the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area, with eight state parks and a waterfall in most.

title: Skate the Chain of Lakes when it freezes
description: The city ploughs rinks straight onto the lake ice and leaves them free and open. Locals treat it as a commute, not an outing.

title: Follow the Blues Trail through the Delta
description: Markers at the places the music actually came from, and juke joints in Clarksdale that still put a band on midweek.

title: Walk the siege lines at Vicksburg
description: Forty-seven days of siege ended on 4 July 1863 and split the Confederacy in two. The park road runs along both armies' earthworks.

title: Float the Current River
description: Spring-fed and cold enough to be a shock in August, through the first river system in the country protected as a national park unit.

title: Eat Kansas City barbecue at a burnt-ends counter
description: Burnt ends began as offcuts given away at the end of the brisket. Now people queue for them, which the original butchers would find funny.

title: Soak outdoors at Chico Hot Springs
description: An 1900 hot spring resort in Paradise Valley, open all year, and at its best when it is snowing on you.

title: Walk the Little Bighorn battlefield
description: White markers where the Seventh Cavalry fell, and since 2003 a memorial to the Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho who beat them.

title: Walk the Flume Gorge boardwalk
description: A 240-metre granite cleft with walls 27 metres high, walked on a boardwalk bolted into the rock since 1808.

title: Walk colonial Portsmouth and eat on the waterfront
description: One of the oldest towns in the country, small enough to cross in twenty minutes, with a working harbour still at the end of the street.

title: Watch synchronous fireflies at Elkmont
description: One of very few places on earth where fireflies flash in unison, for about two weeks in June. Access is by lottery.

title: See the Biltmore Estate and its grounds
description: The largest privately owned house in the United States at 16,000 square metres, with grounds laid out by the man who designed Central Park.

title: Stargaze in one of the darkest skies in the lower 48
description: Western North Dakota has almost no light domes at all. On a clear moonless night the Milky Way casts a shadow.

title: See the geographic centre of North America marker
description: A stone obelisk on a claim first made in 1931 by a rough calculation, disputed ever since, and cheerfully signposted anyway.

title: Walk to Old Man's Cave
description: A blackhand sandstone gorge of recess caves and waterfalls, cut into the one corner of Ohio the glaciers missed. Free.

title: See where the Wright brothers actually worked
description: The bicycle shop and the print works, not the beach at Kitty Hawk. Free, and the aircraft are at the Air Force museum up the road.

title: Watch WaterFire burn on the rivers
description: Eighty braziers lit on the water at sunset on scheduled nights and tended by crews in black boats. Free to watch.

title: Cycle around Block Island
description: Ten square miles reached by ferry, with 45 per cent of it under conservation and bluffs 45 metres above the Atlantic.

title: Walk the boardwalk under the champion trees
description: The largest old-growth bottomland hardwood forest left in the country, with some of the tallest trees in eastern North America. Free.

title: Hear Gullah Geechee history in the Lowcountry
description: The Penn Center was one of the first schools for freed people in the South, and the language and cooking of the sea islands are still their own.

title: Walk or ski the Stowe Recreation Path
description: Eight kilometres of paved path along the West Branch, free, and groomed for cross-country skiing once the snow comes.

title: Watch the sun set over Lake Champlain
description: The Adirondacks on the far shore turn the whole lake orange. The bike path along the waterfront runs out onto a causeway into the lake.

title: Visit the telescope in the National Radio Quiet Zone
description: Thirty-three thousand square kilometres where mobile phones and wifi are restricted by law, so a 100-metre dish can listen across the galaxy.

title: Raft the Gauley during the autumn dam releases
description: Twenty-two weekend days a year when the Summersville dam releases, turning the river into some of the hardest commercially run water in the country.

title: Eat at a Door County fish boil
description: Whitefish and potatoes boiled over an open fire, finished by throwing kerosene on the flames so the oil boils over the rim.

title: Eat cheese curds that squeak at the Dane County market
description: The largest producer-only farmers' market in the country, around the Capitol square. If the curds do not squeak they are not fresh.

title: Scramble to the summit of Old Rag
description: A granite scramble with real hand-over-hand sections near the top. Day-use tickets are capped and must be booked ahead.

title: Walk colonial Williamsburg out of season
description: The largest living history museum in the country. In winter the crowds go and the interpreters have time to talk properly.

title: Cycle the Tony Knowles Coastal Trail
description: Eighteen kilometres from downtown Anchorage along the Cook Inlet mudflats, with belugas offshore and the occasional moose on the path. Free.

title: Walk to the face of the Mendenhall Glacier
description: A glacier reachable on a city bus, with a free lakeside trail to a waterfall beside the ice. The visitor centre charges; the trail does not.

title: Walk the Wynwood murals
description: A warehouse district turned open-air gallery from 2009. The surrounding streets are free; only the walled courtyard is ticketed.

title: Drive Loop Road through Big Cypress at dusk
description: Forty kilometres of gravel through cypress swamp with alligators on the verge and barred owls calling. Free, and far quieter than the Everglades road.

title: Board the last wooden whaleship at Mystic Seaport
description: The Charles W Morgan, launched 1841, is the only wooden whaleship left afloat anywhere. The yard around her still builds and repairs by hand.

title: See the Gutenberg Bible at the Beinecke
description: Walls of translucent marble filter daylight onto a glass tower of books six storeys high. Free, and one of the strangest interiors in the country.

title: Drive the Litchfield Hills in October
description: White clapboard greens and covered bridges through the north-west corner, close enough to New York that people forget it is quiet.

title: See where Mark Twain wrote Huckleberry Finn
description: A nineteen-room Gothic house he designed himself and went bankrupt keeping. Harriet Beecher Stowe lived next door.

title: Take the boat around the Thimble Islands
description: An archipelago of pink granite outcrops off Stony Creek, some holding a single house, quarried for the stone in Grand Central Station.

title: Walk the Appalachian Trail along the Housatonic
description: The longest riverwalk section of the entire Appalachian Trail runs flat beside the water here for about eight kilometres. Free.

title: Watch the Coast Guard barque Eagle come in
description: A 1936 German-built square rigger taken as war reparations, still the training ship, and open to visitors when she is alongside.

title: Eat oysters where they are dredged
description: Long Island Sound oysters are farmed on beds worked since the 1800s, and the boats land at the same dock the restaurants sit on.

title: Walk the Rehoboth boardwalk out of season
description: A mile of boards, free, and in October the summer crowds are gone but the fudge shops are still open.

title: Cycle Cape Henlopen to the point
description: Second World War observation towers still stand in the dunes, built to spot U-boats off the Delaware Bay.

title: See the du Pont gardens at Longwood
description: A thousand acres of designed landscape around a house holding ninety thousand pieces of American decorative art.

title: Stand on the Green where Delaware ratified first
description: On 7 December 1787 Delaware became the first state, which is why the number one is on the number plates. The Green is unchanged and free.

title: Watch the shorebird migration at Bombay Hook
description: Tidal salt marsh on the Atlantic flyway, with a twelve-mile driving loop and hundreds of thousands of birds passing through in spring.

title: Paddle the Nanticoke River cypress swamp
description: The northernmost stand of bald cypress in the country, paddled between trunks in water the colour of tea.

title: Ride the Wilmington and Western steam train
description: A volunteer-run 1872 branch line through the Red Clay Valley, pulled by steam on scheduled weekends.

title: Eat scrapple for breakfast without flinching
description: Pork scraps and cornmeal, sliced and fried until the edges go crisp. A Mid-Atlantic breakfast that people either grew up with or refuse.

title: Kiss the bricks at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway
description: A metre of the original 1909 brick surface is left at the start-finish line, and winners kiss it. The track tour drives you round it.

title: Climb Mount Baldy at Indiana Dunes
description: A moving sand dune on the Lake Michigan shore with a steel mill on one horizon and Chicago on the other.

title: Walk Brown County State Park in October
description: The largest state park in Indiana, in hills the glaciers missed, and the best autumn colour in the Midwest outside New England.

title: Walk the modernist architecture of Columbus
description: A town of 50,000 with buildings by Saarinen, Pei and Roche, because one local industrialist paid the architects' fees for four decades.

title: Go underground at Marengo Cave
description: Found in 1883 by two children who climbed down a sinkhole with a candle. A national landmark, and still privately run.

title: Cycle the Pufferbelly and Rivergreenway trails
description: Forty kilometres of free path along three rivers through the middle of the city.

title: Watch the Little 500 bike race
description: Two hundred laps on a cinder track by student teams on identical single-speed bikes, run since 1951 and the reason Breaking Away exists.

title: Buy pie in northern Indiana Amish country
description: One of the largest Amish settlements in the country, with a Tuesday auction that has run since 1922 and buggies on the road shoulder.

title: Ride the Fenelon Place elevator
description: Ninety metres of cable car up a bluff, built in 1882 by a banker who wanted to get home for lunch. Three states visible at the top.

title: Drive the Loess Hills scenic byway
description: Wind-blown silt piled into hills up to sixty metres deep, a landform found at this scale in only one other place on earth, in China.

title: Find the covered bridges of Madison County
description: Six of the original nineteen survive, roofed to protect the timber trusses rather than the travellers. Free to visit, all of them.

title: Walk the bear and bird mounds above the Mississippi
description: Two hundred earthworks built between 1400 and 750 years ago, some shaped like animals and only readable from the bluff above.

title: Eat your way through the Iowa State Fair
description: The butter cow has been sculpted every year since 1911. Around eighty foods are sold on a stick, which is the point.

title: Walk the Amana Colonies
description: Seven villages founded in 1855 by German pietists who held everything in common until 1932, and still make the furniture and the wine.

title: Swim in the Iowa Great Lakes
description: One of only three blue-water glacial lakes in the world by the local reckoning, and where the whole state seems to go in July.

title: See the tulips at Pella in May
description: Three hundred thousand bulbs and a working Dutch windmill, in a town settled by Dutch dissenters in 1847.

title: Drive the Flint Hills Scenic Byway
description: The last large stand of tallgrass prairie on earth, saved because the ground is too rocky to plough. In June the grass is over your head.

title: Walk the Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve
description: Four thousand hectares with a bison herd, a stone barn from 1881, and nothing on the horizon in any direction. Free.

title: See the Garden of Eden folk art at Lucas
description: A Civil War veteran spent twenty-two years covering his log-cabin plot in concrete sculpture about labour and capital. He is buried in it.

title: Stand under Monument Rocks on the high plains
description: Chalk pillars twenty metres high left by an inland sea, on private land the owners let people visit free, down eight kilometres of dirt road.

title: Walk Boot Hill and the Santa Fe Trail ruts
description: Wagon ruts from the Santa Fe Trail are still visible west of town, cut deep enough by 1870 to survive a century and a half of weather.

title: Cycle the Arkansas River path in Wichita
description: Free paved path along both banks, past the Keeper of the Plains sculpture where the two rivers meet and fire pots are lit at dusk.

title: See real Mercury and Apollo hardware at the Cosmosphere
description: Hutchinson holds the largest collection of Russian space artefacts outside Moscow, and the actual Apollo 13 command module.

title: Eat steak at the Grand Central Hotel
description: Flint Hills beef eaten in the county it was raised in, on a brick main street ending at a French-roofed courthouse from 1873.

title: Eat crab with a mallet and Old Bay
description: Blue crab steamed and tipped onto brown paper. You are given a mallet and no cutlery, and it takes about three hours to eat properly.

title: See the wild ponies on Assateague Island
description: A feral herd on a barrier island, managed by fence into a Maryland group and a Virginia group. Camping here means securing your food properly.

title: Walk the Naval Academy and the state house
description: The oldest state house still in legislative use, where Washington resigned his commission in 1783. The dome is loblolly pine, no nails.

title: Sail a skipjack on the Chesapeake
description: The last commercial sailing fleet in North America, still dredging oysters under sail because the law requires it on certain days.

title: Cycle the Great Allegheny Passage
description: Two hundred and forty kilometres of former railway, joining the C&O towpath so you can ride from Pittsburgh to Washington without a road.

title: Ski or paddle at Deep Creek Lake
description: Western Maryland is high enough for real snow, so the same lake is a ski weekend in February and a swimming one in July.

title: Look for shark teeth under Calvert Cliffs
description: Miocene cliffs eroding into the bay, shedding fossil teeth onto the beach after every storm. A two-mile walk in from the car park.

title: Walk the Antietam battlefield at dawn
description: The bloodiest single day in American history, 17 September 1862. The farmland is kept as it was, which is what makes it land.

title: Watch half a million sandhill cranes on the Platte
description: Eighty per cent of the world's sandhill cranes stop on eighty kilometres of river each March. From a blind at dawn it is deafening.

title: See Carhenge
description: Stonehenge built from thirty-nine grey-painted American cars in 1987 as a memorial to the builder's father. Free, and open always.

title: Walk to the top of Scotts Bluff
description: A landmark on the Oregon Trail visible for a day's travel in either direction. Wagon ruts are still cut into the ground below it.

title: Drive the Sandhills Journey byway
description: Fifty thousand square kilometres of grass-stabilised dune, the largest such formation in the western hemisphere, and almost nobody on the road.

title: Walk the badlands at Toadstool Geologic Park
description: Mushroom-shaped rock in dry badlands, with a mammoth-kill site nearby and a campground of eight spots and no water.

title: See the big cats at Henry Doorly Zoo
description: The largest indoor desert and the largest indoor rainforest in the world, in a city that keeps quietly funding it.

title: See Chimney Rock from the trail route
description: The most mentioned landmark in overland trail diaries. It has eroded measurably since, so what you see is smaller than what they described.

title: Tank the Niobrara River
description: Floating a stretch of river in a livestock tank is a genuine Nebraska tradition, past two hundred waterfalls falling off the valley side.

title: Watch the autumn raptor migration at Cape May
description: The peninsula funnels migrating birds to its tip before they cross the bay. On a good September day the hawk count runs into thousands.

title: Paddle the cedar water of the Pine Barrens
description: Four thousand square kilometres of pine forest over an aquifer, with water stained red by cedar and iron, an hour from Philadelphia.

title: See a band at the Stone Pony
description: Open since 1974 and still a working room rather than a shrine, on a boardwalk that has been derelict and rebuilt twice since.

title: Walk to Mount Tammany at the Water Gap
description: A steep red-dot climb to a view straight down the notch the river cut through the ridge. Free, busy at weekends, worth an early start.

title: Cycle the Delaware and Raritan Canal towpath
description: Seventy kilometres of flat gravel towpath from Trenton to New Brunswick, past locks still worked by hand for the water supply.

title: Walk the Absecon Lighthouse and the boardwalk
description: Two hundred and twenty-eight steps up the tallest lighthouse in New Jersey, built in 1857 after a run of wrecks on the bar.

title: Eat a pork roll and look at Manhattan
description: The state argues about whether it is pork roll or Taylor ham depending on which half you are in. The skyline view is free either way.

title: Walk the undeveloped dunes at Island Beach
description: Sixteen kilometres of barrier island left as it was, with ospreys nesting and a maritime forest behind the primary dune.

title: Sit at the Oklahoma City National Memorial
description: One hundred and sixty-eight empty chairs, one for each person killed on 19 April 1995, nineteen of them small. The reflecting pool is free to visit.

title: Look for bison in the Wichita Mountains
description: Granite hills full of free-roaming bison, elk and longhorn, on one of the oldest refuges in the country. Free entry.

title: Walk the art deco of downtown Tulsa
description: Oil money built one of the densest collections of art deco in America between 1920 and 1935, and most of it is still standing.

title: Understand the Greenwood massacre where it happened
description: Black Wall Street was destroyed from the air and by mob over two days in 1921. The rebuilt district now carries the history openly.

title: Follow Route 66 across Oklahoma
description: More original alignment survives here than in any other state, including a stretch of the 1926 nine-foot-wide Ribbon Road.

title: Swim in the Beavers Bend clearwater
description: Cold clear water released from the bottom of a dam, in pine forest that feels like Arkansas rather than the plains.

title: Stand on Black Mesa, the highest point in Oklahoma
description: A lava-capped mesa at 1,516 metres in the far panhandle, thirteen kilometres return, with dinosaur tracks in the valley below.

title: Walk the Tallgrass Prairie Preserve at Pawhuska
description: Nineteen thousand hectares of restored prairie on the Osage Nation with around two thousand bison. Free, and the road through is gravel.

title: Board the USS Alabama at Mobile Bay
description: A South Dakota-class battleship that earned nine battle stars and was saved by Alabama schoolchildren collecting coins in 1964.

title: Walk Kelly Ingram Park and the Civil Rights Institute
description: The park where police turned dogs and hoses on schoolchildren in 1963, across the road from the church where four girls were killed that September.

title: Swim the falls at Little River Canyon
description: One of the few rivers in the country that runs its whole length on top of a mountain, cutting a gorge 200 metres deep. Free.

title: Watch the spring bird fallout on Dauphin Island
description: First land after a 900km Gulf crossing, so an April storm can drop thousands of exhausted songbirds into a few hectares of scrub.

title: Stand outside Little Rock Central High
description: Still a working school. Nine students walked in past a mob and the National Guard in 1957; the visitor centre opposite tells it plainly.

title: See the American art at Crystal Bridges
description: Safdie pavilions built over a ravine, holding American art from colonial portraits to Rothko, and free to enter permanently.

title: Walk to Hawksbill Crag
description: A cantilevered stone beak over the Buffalo River valley, five kilometres return down a forest road most hire cars will manage in the dry.

title: Walk the whole town of Eureka Springs
description: A Victorian spa town built into a hillside so steep no street crosses another at a right angle, and the whole of it is on the historic register.

title: Drive to the highest point in Arkansas
description: Eight hundred and thirty-nine metres, with hang gliders launching off the south bluff and black bear in the woods below.

title: Walk the memorials after dark
description: Lincoln, Korea and Vietnam are open and lit all night, and are entirely different places without the daytime crowds. Free.

title: See the Library of Congress reading room
description: The largest library in the world by shelf length. The Great Hall is free; the reading room floor needs a reader card, which is also free.

title: Walk under the cherry trees before the crowds
description: Three thousand trees given by Tokyo in 1912. Peak bloom lasts about four days and is forecast weeks ahead; go at sunrise.

title: Eat a half-smoke at Ben's Chili Bowl
description: Open on U Street since 1958, through the 1968 riots and the years afterwards when almost nothing else on the street stayed open.

title: See the Hope Diamond and the whale at Natural History
place: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
description: Free, like every Smithsonian, and big enough that picking two halls beats trying to see it all.

title: Float the Boise River through town
description: Ten kilometres from Barber Park to Ann Morrison on a tube, with a shuttle bus back. The city treats it as summer transport.

title: Ski or ride Bald Mountain at Sun Valley
description: The first destination ski resort in America, and the chairlift was invented here in 1936 by an engineer who had been loading bananas onto ships.

title: Raft the Middle Fork of the Salmon
description: A hundred and sixty kilometres through the largest roadless area in the lower 48, with hot springs on the bank and permits by lottery.

title: Cycle the Trail of the Coeur d'Alenes
description: A hundred and twelve kilometres of paved former railway across the panhandle, laid over a mining superfund site that was capped beneath it.

title: Soak in a wild hot spring near Stanley
description: Boat Box is a steel tub on the riverbank you fill by bucket. Free, first come, and the Sawtooths are across the water.

title: Hear brass on Frenchmen Street
description: Three blocks of small rooms where the city actually goes to hear music, ten minutes' walk from Bourbon Street and nothing like it.

title: See the salt dome and the egret rookery at Avery Island
description: Tabasco has been made on the same salt dome since 1868, and the founder's son built a bird sanctuary that saved the snowy egret from plume hunters.

title: Walk under the Evangeline Oak in Cajun country
description: The Acadian deportation ended here for many families. The town still speaks Louisiana French in places and dances to it on Saturdays.

title: Go up the Louisiana State Capitol tower
description: The tallest state capitol in the country at 137 metres, built by Huey Long in fourteen months, who was shot in its corridor in 1935.

title: Eat crawfish at a boil in season
description: Boiled with corn, potato and enough cayenne to matter, tipped onto a newspaper table. Season runs roughly February to June.

title: Eat at the Portland working waterfront
description: A fishing pier that never turned into a theme, with the boats unloading beside the restaurants that buy from them.

title: Sail on a Maine windjammer
description: A fleet of restored nineteenth-century schooners that take passengers for several days with no engine and no fixed itinerary.

title: Climb Katahdin by the Knife Edge
description: The northern end of the Appalachian Trail. The Knife Edge is a metre wide in places with a long drop on both sides, and reservations are required.

title: Stand at the easternmost point in the United States
description: A candy-striped lighthouse at the first place in the country the sun touches, with whales in the Bay of Fundy offshore.

title: Look for moose at dawn near Moosehead Lake
description: Maine has the largest moose population in the lower 48. Dawn and dusk on the logging roads north of Greenville is where you see them.

title: See the Diego Rivera murals at the DIA
description: Twenty-seven panels on the Ford Rouge plant, painted 1932, that Rivera considered his best work. The city nearly sold them in bankruptcy.

title: Chase waterfalls to Tahquamenon
description: Root beer coloured from cedar tannin, sixty metres wide, and one of the largest falls east of the Mississippi.

title: Follow the Leelanau wine and cherry route
description: Lake Michigan moderates the peninsula enough to grow riesling, on ground that also produces most of the country's tart cherries.

title: Take the ferry to Isle Royale
description: The least visited national park in the lower 48, closed all winter, with a wolf and moose study running since 1958.

title: See the ice caves and frozen shore at Marquette
description: In a cold enough winter the spray freezes into curtains along the cliffs. Conditions change fast, so ask locally before walking on anything.

title: Cross the Stone Arch Bridge at St Anthony Falls
description: The only stone arch bridge on the whole Mississippi, built for the railway in 1883 and now for people. Free.

title: Paddle and camp in Voyageurs National Park
description: A park you can only really reach by water, on the fur trade route, with campsites accessible by boat alone.

title: Watch a laker come under the Aerial Lift Bridge
description: Thousand-foot ore carriers pass under a bridge that lifts in a minute. Arrival times are published, and the whole thing is free to watch.

title: Look into the Hull-Rust mine at Hibbing
description: Five kilometres long and 180 metres deep, the largest open pit iron mine in the world, and the town was moved to get at the ore.

title: Ride the coasters inside the Mall of America
description: An indoor theme park with roller coasters under a glass roof, which in a Minnesota January is a more reasonable idea than it sounds.

title: Walk Rowan Oak, where Faulkner wrote
description: His outline for A Fable is still pencilled on the study wall. The house is kept as he left it, in woods on the edge of town.

title: Take the boat to Ship Island
description: A barrier island twenty kilometres offshore with white sand, a Civil War fort, and no development of any kind.

title: See the two-room house Elvis was born in
description: Built by his father for 180 dollars. The scale of it is the thing that lands, more than anything at Graceland.

title: Eat hot tamales in the Mississippi Delta
description: A Delta tradition since Mexican labourers worked the cotton fields, sold from stands and simmered rather than steamed.

title: Walk the bluff and the antebellum houses at Natchez
description: More antebellum houses than anywhere in the South, on a bluff above the river, with the histories of the people who built them told alongside.

title: Wander the City Museum
description: A ten-storey former shoe factory turned into a climbable sculpture of salvage: aeroplanes on the roof, caves, and slides between floors.

title: See the caves under Silver Dollar City
description: The cathedral room is 61 metres high, and the theme park above it exists because the family needed to fund the cave tours.

title: Cycle the Katy Trail across Missouri
description: Three hundred and seventy kilometres of former railway, the longest developed rail trail in the country, much of it beside the Missouri River.

title: Scramble the granite at Elephant Rocks
description: Billion-year-old granite weathered into boulders the size of houses, with a braille trail built in 1972 that was among the first anywhere.

title: Swim in the blue water at Ha Ha Tonka
description: A collapsed cave system of sinkholes and natural bridges under the ruin of a castle a Kansas City businessman never finished.

title: Float the Clark Fork through Missoula
description: A town where people finish work and get in the river. There is a surf wave in Brennan's Wave right in the middle of it.

title: Drive the Bitterroot Valley to Lost Trail Pass
description: Lewis and Clark came through here half-starved in 1805. The mountains on the west side rise straight out of the valley floor.

title: Swim in Flathead Lake
description: The largest natural freshwater lake west of the Mississippi, clear enough to see the bottom at ten metres, and cold until late July.

title: See the Charles M Russell collection
description: The cowboy artist's own log studio stands beside the museum, and he painted the West from having actually worked in it.

title: Paddle or watch the Truckee River whitewater park
description: Eleven drop pools engineered through downtown Reno, free to use, with a wave that holds a kayak in place.

title: Swim at Sand Harbor on Lake Tahoe
description: Granite boulders and water clear to twenty metres on the Nevada shore, at 1,900 metres so it never gets warm.

title: Drive the ghost towns of the Nevada silver belt
description: Goldfield had 20,000 people in 1906 and has about 250 now, with the hotel, the courthouse and the school still standing on the highway.

title: See the Fly Geyser on a Friends of Black Rock walk
description: An accidental geyser from a 1964 drilling mishap, built up into mounds of red and green thermophile. Access is by booked walk only.

title: Ride the MS Mount Washington on Winnipesaukee
description: A 1888 route still run daily across the biggest lake in the state, calling at towns that have no road bridge between them.

title: Ride the Cannon Mountain tramway
description: The first aerial tramway in North America, opened 1938. The Old Man of the Mountain fell off this cliff in 2003 and is remembered below.

title: Climb Mount Monadnock
description: Among the most climbed mountains in the world, and a bare summit because farmers burned the trees off it twice in the 1800s.

title: Paddle Great Bay at high tide
description: An inland tidal estuary where half the water leaves twice a day, with oyster restoration beds and wintering eagles.

title: Board the USS North Carolina
description: A battleship you can go nine decks down inside, from the boiler rooms to the sick bay, with very little roped off.

title: Stand where the Wright brothers flew
description: Markers show all four flights of 17 December 1903. The first was twelve seconds and shorter than the wingspan of a 747.

title: Raft the Nantahala Gorge
description: Cold dam-release water through a gorge so narrow the sun reaches the bottom for only a few hours. Good for a first river.

title: Drive to the highest point east of the Mississippi
description: Two thousand and thirty-seven metres, with spruce-fir forest that belongs in Canada and weather to match. Free.

title: Ride the Cuyahoga Valley Scenic Railroad
description: A national park between Cleveland and Akron, with a train that will carry your bike one way so you ride the towpath back.

title: Walk the Great Serpent Mound
description: Four hundred and eleven metres of earthwork in the shape of a snake, on the rim of a meteor crater, aligned to the summer solstice sunset.

title: Take the ferry to Kelleys Island glacial grooves
description: The largest exposed glacial grooves in the world, gouged into limestone by ice eighteen thousand years ago.

title: Eat at the North Market
description: A public market since 1876, and where Jeni's ice cream started before it went national.

title: Ride the Duquesne Incline
description: An 1877 funicular up Mount Washington, still with its original wooden cars, to the view of the three rivers meeting.

title: Eat a cheesesteak and argue about where
description: Whiz, provolone or American, onions or not. The two famous places face each other across an intersection and neither is the local answer.

title: Drive the back roads of Lancaster County
description: The oldest Amish settlement in the country. Buggies use the shoulder, so pass slowly and wide, and nothing is open on a Sunday.

title: Walk to Bushkill Falls
description: Eight falls linked by boardwalk and stairs in a private glen that has charged admission since 1904 and kept the paths in good order.

title: Tour The Breakers
description: Seventy rooms built for the Vanderbilts in two years, with a great hall 15 metres high. The scale is the argument the Gilded Age was making.

title: Surf or watch the break at Narragansett Town Beach
description: The most consistent surf in New England, and one of the few town beaches in the country that charges walk-on admission.

title: Eat at Federal Hill
description: An Italian quarter with a pinecone hung over the entrance arch, and bakeries that have been in the same families for a century.

title: Walk out to Beavertail Light
description: The third oldest lighthouse site in the country on a rocky point, free, and the best storm-watching in the state.

title: Walk Huntington Beach and the alligator boardwalk
description: Considered the best birding on the coast, with a causeway where alligators lie a few metres from the road.

title: Walk the Falls Park suspension bridge
description: A four-lane bridge was demolished in 2002 to uncover the waterfall it had been hiding, and a curved footbridge put over it instead.

title: Walk the boneyard beach at Botany Bay
description: Dead oaks and palmettos standing in the surf where the sea has taken the land. Free, closed Tuesdays, and you may take nothing off the beach.

title: Climb Table Rock in the upcountry
description: Twelve kilometres return and 640 metres of climb up a granite dome, with the Blue Ridge escarpment laid out at the top.

title: Drive the Needles Highway
description: Granite spires and tunnels cut so tight that buses cannot pass. It was called impossible before it was built in 1922.

title: Go down into Wind Cave
description: One of the longest caves in the world and the densest known boxwork formation anywhere, under prairie with bison on top.

title: Walk the falls in the middle of Sioux Falls
description: Seven thousand litres a second over pink quartzite in the middle of the city, with the ruins of a 1881 mill beside it. Free.

title: See the Crazy Horse Memorial in progress
description: Begun in 1948, still unfinished, and funded without government money by choice. The face alone is larger than all of Rushmore.

title: Paddle the Missouri National Recreational River
description: One of the last stretches of the Missouri still braiding across sandbars the way Lewis and Clark described it.

title: Ride the Incline Railway up Lookout Mountain
description: A 72.7 per cent grade at the top, which is about as steep as a passenger railway gets anywhere.

title: Eat dry-rub ribs in Memphis
description: Memphis argues for dry rub where the rest of the South argues for sauce, and the barbecue contest each May is taken very seriously.

title: Walk to the Fiery Gizzard trail bluffs
description: Regularly named among the toughest and best day hikes in the east, through boulder fields and hemlock gorge on the plateau rim.

title: Drive the Bighorn Scenic Byway
description: A range Yellowstone traffic drives straight past, with a medicine wheel at 2,900 metres built by Plains peoples and still in use.

title: Soak in the free state bath at Thermopolis
description: The 1896 treaty transferring the spring required that some of it stay free to everyone forever, and the state still honours it.

title: Watch a rodeo in Wyoming
description: Small-town rodeo is a working sport here rather than a show, and the July nights in Sheridan and Cody are when to see it.

title: See the wood chipper at the Fargo visitor centre
description: The actual prop from the film, kept behind glass with a hat you can borrow for the photograph. Free, and the town leans into it.

title: Walk On-A-Slant Indian Village at Fort Lincoln
description: Reconstructed Mandan earth lodges on a village site occupied for two centuries, beside the fort Custer rode out from in 1876.

title: Cross into the International Peace Garden
description: A garden straddling the border since 1932, where you can walk between two countries. Bring a passport to leave from either side.

title: Drive the Enchanted Highway sculptures
description: Thirty-two miles of county road with the world's largest scrap-metal sculptures beside it, built by one man to keep his town alive.

title: Ice fish on Devils Lake
description: A lake with no outlet that has quadrupled in size since 1993, drowning farms. In winter the ice roads carry trucks and fish houses.

title: See the Dells sandstone from the water
description: Narrow sandstone gorges cut by a glacial flood, photographed by H H Bennett in the 1800s, which is why the tourism happened at all.

title: See the Calatrava wings open at the Milwaukee Art Museum
description: A 27-metre brise soleil that opens at ten, closes at five and flaps once at noon, over a gallery on the lakefront.

title: See the Circus World collection at Baraboo
description: The Ringling Brothers wintered here from 1884, and the largest collection of circus wagons in the world is in the original buildings.

title: Climb the East Bluff at Devil's Lake
description: Quartzite bluffs 150 metres above a lake with no inlet or outlet, dammed at both ends by glacial moraine.

title: Take the Lambeau Field tour
description: The oldest continually operating NFL stadium, in a town of 105,000 that owns its own club through shareholders who get no dividend.

title: Ride the Cass Scenic Railroad up Bald Knob
description: Shay geared locomotives built for logging, climbing an eleven per cent grade to the third highest point in the state.

title: Walk to Jefferson Rock at Harpers Ferry
description: Where two rivers and three states meet, and where John Brown's raid in 1859 helped bring on the war. The lower town is kept as it was.

title: Look up at Seneca Rocks
description: A quartzite fin standing 275 metres above the valley, the only true summit in the east that requires technical climbing to reach.

title: See Blackwater Falls in the Canaan Valley
description: Amber water from hemlock tannin over a 17-metre drop, in a high valley that holds snow when the rest of the state has none.

title: Go down the Beckley Exhibition Coal Mine
description: A retired miner drives you 450 metres into a seam and explains the work. It is the honest counterweight to the scenery above ground.

title: Tour the Ben and Jerry's factory
description: Thirty minutes, a sample at the end, and a flavour graveyard outside with headstones for the discontinued.

title: Walk Mount Tom above Woodstock
description: The only national park telling the story of conservation forestry, on a hillside replanted in the 1870s after Vermont was logged bare.

title: See the steamboat inside the Shelburne Museum
description: Thirty-nine buildings moved onto one site, including a 67-metre Lake Champlain steamboat hauled overland in 1955.

title: Drive the Northeast Kingdom in October
description: The emptiest corner of the state, named by a senator in 1949, where the colour peaks a week before the rest of New England.

title: Ski Killington into May
description: The longest season in the east, usually opening in October and closing after the rest have melted, on six mountains.

title: Walk Lincoln's Springfield
description: The only house he ever owned, on a block kept as it was in the 1860s. Free, with timed tickets from the visitor centre.

title: Walk the Garden of the Gods in Shawnee forest
description: Sandstone weathered into stacked slabs above the forest canopy in the far south, closer to Kentucky than Chicago and nothing like either.

title: Walk the canyons at Starved Rock
description: Eighteen sandstone canyons cut by glacial meltwater, with waterfalls after rain and frozen falls in a hard January.

title: Climb Monks Mound at Cahokia
description: The largest earthwork in the Americas, at the centre of a city of perhaps twenty thousand people in 1100 AD, larger than London then.

title: See how a Louisville Slugger is turned
description: Bats made on the same site since 1884, still turned to order for players, with a 36-metre steel bat leaning on the building.

title: See the moonbow at Cumberland Falls
description: One of very few places in the world with a predictable lunar rainbow, visible on clear nights around the full moon.

title: Watch the elk and bison at Land Between the Lakes
description: A restored prairie herd on a peninsula between two reservoirs, with a driving loop and a dark sky observatory nearby.

title: Drive the horse farms around Lexington
description: Limestone under the pasture puts calcium in the grass, which is the reason the thoroughbred industry settled exactly here.

title: Walk into Providence Canyon
description: Gullies up to 45 metres deep cut entirely by bad farming practice in the 1800s. A man-made accident that became the state's canyon.

title: Walk to Amicalola Falls
description: The tallest cascade in the south-east at 222 metres, with 604 steps beside it and the Appalachian Trail approach starting at the top.

title: See a band in Athens
description: R.E.M. and the B-52s came out of the same few blocks, and the 40 Watt Club still books new bands most nights of the week.

title: Walk Driftwood Beach on Jekyll Island
description: A boneyard beach of bleached oaks killed by erosion, best at low tide, on an island the state bought in 1947 to keep public.

title: Drive the Blue Ridge Parkway from Roanoke
description: Three peaks over a lake at milepost 86, with a walk up Sharp Top on a shuttle bus if you would rather not climb it.

title: See the stalacpipe organ at Luray Caverns
description: Rubber mallets strike stalactites across 14,000 square metres to play music, which makes it the largest instrument on earth.

title: Walk False Cape by foot or bike only
description: Reachable only on foot, by bike or by boat, which is why nine kilometres of Atlantic beach here stay empty in July.

title: Walk Monticello and the enslaved quarters
description: Jefferson's house and, since 2018, the restored Mulberry Row where the people he enslaved lived and worked. Both are the tour now.

title: Cycle Nantucket to Sconset
description: Cobbled streets, a whaling museum, and a flat bike path to a village of rose-covered cottages at the far end.

title: Walk Salem outside October
description: The witch trial memorial is a quiet stone bench court. In October the town is unusable; any other month it is a serious maritime port.

title: Walk around Walden Pond
description: A kettle pond with a marked cabin site and a swimming beach. Parking is capped, so arrive early on a summer weekend.

title: Ride a swan boat in the Public Garden
description: Pedal-powered by one person hidden in the swan since 1877, run by the same family the whole time.

title: Drive the North Cascades Highway
description: Closed by avalanche risk from November to spring. Diablo Lake is turquoise from glacial flour ground off the rock above it.

title: Walk the Enchantments day route
description: Thirty-two kilometres point to point over Aasgard Pass, or an overnight if you win the permit lottery. Mountain goats will follow you.

title: Walk the Georgia O'Keeffe landscape at Ghost Ranch
description: The cliffs she painted for forty years, with a dinosaur quarry on the same property that produced thousands of Coelophysis skeletons.

title: Walk into the Gila Cliff Dwellings
description: Forty rooms built into five caves by Mogollon people in the 1280s and abandoned within a generation. You walk right into them.

title: See a show at Red Rocks
description: Two 90-metre sandstone monoliths forming natural acoustics. Free to walk and use for exercise on any day without a show.

title: Ride the Durango and Silverton narrow gauge
description: Coal-fired steam on 914mm gauge along a ledge above the Animas gorge, running the same route since 1882.

title: Drive the Historic Columbia River Highway
description: The first scenic highway in the country, built 1913 to a grade gentle enough for early cars, past a string of waterfalls.

title: See the bluebonnets in the Hill Country
description: Lady Bird Johnson's roadside planting programme is why the verges go blue for three weeks each spring. Free, and everyone stops.

title: See the riverbanks and the Congaree at Columbia
description: Twenty kilometres of free riverside path where three rivers meet, with the old canal locks still in place along it.

title: Raft the US National Whitewater Center
description: The largest man-made whitewater river in the world, pumped in a loop, and an Olympic training site open to anyone who turns up.

title: Climb an Adirondack High Peak
description: Forty-six summits over 4,000 feet, and a club for anyone who does all of them. Cascade is the usual first one.

title: Drive the farm roads of Little Compton
description: Stone walls, a colonial common and no through traffic, in the corner of the state most Rhode Islanders keep to themselves.

title: Hike below the rim of the Grand Canyon
description: Going down is optional, coming back up is not - rangers pull people off the Bright Angel Trail every summer. Go in spring or autumn.

title: Reach the quieter North Rim of the Grand Canyon
description: Takes about a tenth of the visitors, sits 300m higher, and closes under snow from December. Four hours' drive from the South Rim to go 16km.

title: Raft the Colorado through the Grand Canyon
description: Up to three weeks and 440km through the canyon floor. Private permits run on a weighted lottery with a wait that has run to years.

title: Walk down to Havasu Falls
description: Turquoise water from travertine minerals, 16km down into Havasupai land. Permits sell out within minutes on the February release and are non-transferable.

title: See the light beams in Antelope Canyon
description: A slot canyon on Navajo Nation land, accessible only with a Navajo guide. The shafts of light appear around midday from about March to October.

title: Stand above Horseshoe Bend
description: A 270-degree meander of the Colorado, 300m below an unfenced sandstone rim. Twenty minutes from the car park, and no shade at all.

title: Drive the valley floor at Monument Valley
description: A Navajo tribal park, not a national park - the sandstone buttes John Ford filmed nine times. The 27km loop road is rough but doable in a normal car.

title: Win the lottery for The Wave at Coyote Buttes
description: Undulating Navajo sandstone laid down as dunes 190 million years ago. Only 64 people a day get in, by lottery, and the route is unmarked.

title: Climb Cathedral Rock at sunset in Sedona
description: Iron-stained sandstone spires, a serious short scramble, and a town built around the belief that the rocks emit energy vortexes.

title: Walk among the saguaro at sunset
description: Saguaro grow only in the Sonoran, take 35 years to flower and 75 to sprout an arm. The tallest here are over 12m.

title: See the fossil logs at Petrified Forest
description: 225-million-year-old trees turned to quartz, plus a stretch of original Route 66. One of the very few national parks where dogs can join you on trails.

title: Drive the surviving stretches of Route 66
description: Decommissioned in 1985 and replaced by interstates, but long segments survive as business routes through towns the freeway bypassed.

title: Look into Meteor Crater
description: 1.2km wide and 170m deep, punched out 50,000 years ago and the first crater on earth proven to be from an impact. Apollo crews trained in it.

title: Wade The Narrows in Zion
description: Walking up the Virgin River between 300m walls that close to nine metres apart. Closed whenever flash flood risk is high - check daily.

title: Walk the chains up Angels Landing
description: A 500m spine with chains and drops on both sides. Permits have been required since 2022, by lottery, and the fatality count is in the teens.

title: Walk down among the hoodoos at Bryce Canyon
description: Not a canyon but an eroding escarpment holding the densest concentration of hoodoos on earth. The Navajo Loop takes you between them.

title: Walk to Delicate Arch for sunset
description: The arch on Utah's licence plates - 4.8km return over slickrock with no shade. Arches has held over 2,000 arches and loses one occasionally.

title: Watch sunrise through Mesa Arch at Canyonlands
description: For about twenty minutes at dawn the underside of the arch glows orange from light bouncing off the canyon below.

title: Drive the Burr Trail through Capitol Reef
description: A 160km wrinkle in the earth's crust called the Waterpocket Fold, and the least visited of Utah's five parks. Pick fruit in the Fruita orchards in season.

title: Wander the mushroom rocks at Goblin Valley
description: A valley of squat hoodoos you are actually encouraged to scramble over - rare in a landscape this fragile, and excellent for it.

title: Drive on the Bonneville Salt Flats
description: About 120 square kilometres of salt crust where land speed records have been set since 1912. Wet for much of the year - check before driving on.

title: Find Spiral Jetty on the Great Salt Lake
description: Robert Smithson's 460m basalt coil from 1970, submerged for thirty years and now high and dry as the lake shrinks - which is its own commentary.

title: Sled the gypsum dunes at White Sands
description: 275 square miles of white gypsum sand you can toboggan down. Dogs are allowed on leash almost everywhere here, unusually.

title: Watch the bat flight at Carlsbad Caverns
description: Hundreds of thousands of Brazilian free-tailed bats spiral out of the natural entrance at dusk. Walk in through the same hole rather than taking the lift.

title: Climb the ladders to the cliff dwellings at Bandelier
description: Ancestral Pueblo homes carved into volcanic tuff, occupied for four centuries. Wooden ladders take you up into the alcoves themselves.

title: Walk the adobe streets of Santa Fe
description: Founded in 1610 and the oldest capital in the US, with a building code that has kept the whole centre in adobe. Georgia O'Keeffe's museum is here.

title: Visit Taos Pueblo
description: Continuously inhabited for over 1,000 years - the oldest such community in the US, and still without electricity or running water by choice.

title: See the dishes at the Very Large Array
description: 27 radio dishes, each 25m across, moved along rail tracks into different configurations across a high desert plain. Contact was filmed here.

title: Drive Trail Ridge Road in Rocky Mountain National Park
description: The highest continuous paved road in the US, topping 3,713m, with eighteen kilometres above the treeline. Timed entry applies in summer.

title: See the Maroon Bells reflected at dawn
description: Reputedly the most photographed peaks in North America, and lethal to climb - the mudstone is so loose they are known as the Deadly Bells.

title: Sandboard the Great Sand Dunes
description: The tallest dunes in North America at 230m, against the Sangre de Cristo range, with a seasonal creek at their base you can float down in spring.

title: Tour the Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde
description: 150 rooms built into an alcove by Ancestral Puebloans around 1200 CE and abandoned within a century. Ranger-guided entry only, ladders included.

title: Drive the Million Dollar Highway to Ouray
description: 40km of US 550 over three passes with no guardrails and a sheer drop on the outside lane. Built on an 1880s toll road for the silver mines.

title: Look into the Black Canyon of the Gunnison
description: So narrow and deep that parts of the floor get 33 minutes of sunlight a day. The Painted Wall is the tallest cliff in Colorado at 682m.

title: Watch the Grand Prismatic Spring from the overlook
description: The world's first national park, sitting on an active supervolcano. The overlook trail beats the boardwalk for seeing the colours.

title: Watch wolves at dawn in the Lamar Valley
description: Wolves were reintroduced in 1995 after seventy years' absence, and this valley is where you have the best chance. Bring a spotting scope and get up early.

title: Wait for Old Faithful to go off
description: Erupts every 60 to 110 minutes and is predicted to within ten minutes - the most predictable big geyser anywhere, though not the largest.

title: Paddle Jenny Lake under the Tetons
description: The range rises 2,100m straight off the valley floor with no foothills at all, because the fault runs right along its base.

title: Walk the base trail around Devils Tower
description: The first US national monument, declared in 1906. Sacred to more than twenty tribes, who ask climbers to stay off voluntarily through June.

title: Drive the Going-to-the-Sun Road in Glacier
description: 80km over Logan Pass, only fully open for about ten weeks a year, and now requiring a timed entry reservation in peak season.

title: Walk the Highline Trail along the Garden Wall
description: Cut into a cliff along the Continental Divide, with a hand cable on the exposed opening section and mountain goats using the same path.

title: Walk the lava fields at Craters of the Moon
description: 1,600 square kilometres of basalt flows and lava tubes, last erupted about 2,000 years ago. Apollo astronauts trained here in 1969.

title: See Shoshone Falls at full flow
description: At 65m it is higher than Niagara, but irrigation takes most of the water for much of the year - spring runoff is the only time it performs.

title: Walk to Sawtooth Lake
description: A granite range with over 400 alpine lakes and no road through the middle of it, in one of the largest dark-sky reserves in the country.

title: Walk the Notch Trail in Badlands
description: A wooden ladder up a cliff face leads to a ledge over the White River valley, through eroded sediment laid down 75 million years ago.

title: See the faces at Mount Rushmore
description: Carved 1927-41 into a granite face in the Black Hills - land the Supreme Court ruled in 1980 was taken from the Lakota unlawfully.

title: Drive the Wildlife Loop in Custer State Park
description: A herd of around 1,400 bison, plus the Needles Highway with tunnels cut so tight they have to be measured before you drive them.

title: See the wild horses in Theodore Roosevelt National Park
description: The only national park named for a person, on the ranch land that turned him into a conservationist. Feral horses and bison on the loop road.

title: Walk into Santa Elena Canyon at Big Bend
description: 460m limestone walls with the Rio Grande running between them - the US on one bank, Mexico on the other, close enough to shout across.

title: Watch 1.5 million bats leave Congress Avenue Bridge
description: The largest urban bat colony in the world, roosting in bridge expansion joints and pouring out at dusk from March to October.

title: Queue for brisket in Texas Hill Country
description: Post oak, salt, pepper and about twelve hours. The best places sell out by early afternoon and the queue starts before they open.

title: Walk the River Walk and the Alamo
description: A flood control scheme from the 1930s turned into a river-level promenade, linking to four Spanish missions that are World Heritage listed.

title: Ride into Palo Duro Canyon
description: The second largest canyon in the US, 190km long and up to 240m deep, and almost nobody outside Texas knows it exists.

title: Wait for the Marfa lights
description: Unexplained lights reported since 1883, with a purpose-built viewing area on US 90 - and a town that became a minimalist art destination because Donald Judd moved in.

title: Watch the light hit El Capitan in Yosemite Valley
description: Granite walls a kilometre high above a glacial valley. US national parks restrict dogs to paved areas and campgrounds only.

title: Climb the cables up Half Dome
description: 24km return with 1,460m of climb, finishing on two steel cables up bare granite. Permits are by lottery and people have died on the cables.

title: Catch the Horsetail Fall firefall in February
description: For about two weeks the setting sun lights a thin fall on El Capitan so it glows like molten rock. Needs water in the fall and a cloudless west horizon.

title: Stand under General Sherman in Sequoia National Park
description: The largest tree on earth by volume - 1,487 cubic metres, and still adding the equivalent of a mature tree's worth of wood every year.

title: Climb Mount Whitney, the highest point in the lower 48
description: 4,421m via 35km and 1,900m of ascent, usually done in one brutal day. Day-use permits are a February lottery.

title: Find the movie locations in the Alabama Hills
description: Rounded granite used in more than 400 films, with Mobius Arch framing Whitney behind it. BLM land, so dogs and free camping are both fine.

title: Walk among the tufa towers at Mono Lake
description: Calcium spires exposed when Los Angeles diverted the inflow streams and the lake dropped 14m. A court case in 1994 stopped it going dry.

title: Walk the streets of Bodie ghost town
description: A gold town of 10,000 abandoned to arrested decay - about 100 buildings left standing exactly as found, with goods still on the shop shelves.

title: Watch sunrise over the dunes in Death Valley
description: The hottest place ever reliably recorded at 56.7C, and the lowest in North America at 86m below sea level. Do not come in July.

title: Find the moving rocks at Racetrack Playa
description: Stones that leave trails across the dry lake, finally explained in 2014 as thin ice floating them along. 43km of tyre-shredding washboard to reach.

title: Sleep under the Joshua trees
description: Where the Mojave meets the Colorado desert, with monzogranite boulders, a Dark Sky Park designation and rock climbing everywhere you look.

title: Climb Salvation Mountain
description: Leonard Knight spent nearly thirty years building a hill out of adobe and half a million litres of donated paint, beside the shrinking Salton Sea.

title: Drive Highway 1 through Big Sur
description: 140km of coast road on the edge of the Santa Lucia range. Landslides close sections for months at a time - check before committing.

title: Walk the headlands at Point Lobos
description: Called the greatest meeting of land and water in the world by the painter Francis McComas - sea otters, harbour seals and Monterey cypress.

title: Tour the excess of Hearst Castle
description: 165 rooms built by William Randolph Hearst over 28 years, with a Roman pool lined in gold leaf and a zoo that once held zebras. Some still roam.

title: Stand under the tallest trees on earth in Redwood
description: Coast redwoods reach over 110m. The tallest known tree's location is deliberately unpublished to protect the ground around its roots.

title: Walk across the Golden Gate Bridge
description: 2.7km of art deco steel painted International Orange so it stays visible in fog. September and October are the clearest months.

title: Take the night tour of Alcatraz
description: A federal prison for 29 years, and occupied by Native American activists for 19 months from 1969 - graffiti from that occupation is still on the walls.

title: Ride a cable car up Hyde Street
description: The last manually operated cable car system in the world, running since 1873 by gripping a cable moving under the street at a constant 15km/h.

title: Walk among the old-growth at Muir Woods
description: One of the last uncut coast redwood stands near the coast, saved in 1908. Parking and shuttle must be reserved in advance - no walk-ups.

title: Taste Cabernet in the Napa Valley
description: The 1976 Judgement of Paris, where Napa beat Bordeaux blind, remade the region. Most tastings now need a booking.

title: See the city from Griffith Observatory
description: Free since it opened in 1935, with the Hollywood sign on one side and the whole basin on the other. Go at dusk and stay for the telescope.

title: Walk the Venice Beach boardwalk
description: Built in 1905 as a Californian imitation of Venice, canals included. Now street performers, Muscle Beach and a skate park on the sand.

title: See the tar pits at La Brea
description: Asphalt still seeping in the middle of Los Angeles, having trapped and preserved Ice Age animals for 50,000 years. Excavation continues on site.

title: Kayak the sea caves at La Jolla
description: Seven caves cut into the sandstone cliff, in a marine reserve with leopard sharks in the shallows through summer and sea lions on the rocks.

title: Spend a day in Balboa Park
description: 490 hectares of Spanish Colonial Revival buildings from the 1915 exposition, holding 17 museums and the San Diego Zoo.

title: Swim in Lake Tahoe
description: 501m deep and clear enough to see 20m down, straddling the California and Nevada line. Cold enough that most people manage about four minutes.

title: Look into Crater Lake
description: The deepest lake in the US at 594m, filling a caldera left when Mount Mazama collapsed about 7,700 years ago. Fed only by rain and snow.

title: Walk up to Multnomah Falls
description: 189m in two drops with a 1914 footbridge across the middle. Timed-entry permits apply in summer - book before you drive out.

title: Watch the tide come in at Haystack Rock
description: A 72m sea stack with tufted puffins nesting on it in spring and tide pools at its base. Oregon beaches are public and dog friendly by law.

title: Watch the sea drain into Thor's Well
description: A collapsed sea cave that appears to swallow the ocean. Best an hour either side of high tide - and people have been swept off these rocks.

title: See the Painted Hills change colour
description: Banded claystone recording 35 million years of climate change, and the colours genuinely shift with moisture and light through the day.

title: Climb Misery Ridge at Smith Rock
description: The birthplace of American sport climbing, on welded tuff above a river bend. The ridge trail is short, steep and named accurately.

title: Get lost in Powell's City of Books
description: A city block of new and used books shelved side by side - around a million of them, and the largest independent bookshop in the world.

title: Walk the Hoh Rain Forest in Olympic
description: A temperate rainforest getting up to 4 metres of rain a year, with moss hanging off every branch - and glaciers and coast in the same park.

title: Walk through Hole-in-the-Wall at Rialto Beach
description: Driftwood logs the size of telegraph poles, sea stacks in the mist, and an arch you can only reach at low tide. Check the tide table, seriously.

title: See the wildflowers at Paradise on Mount Rainier
description: An active volcano carrying more glacial ice than the rest of the lower 48 combined, with a six-week meadow bloom at its foot.

title: Watch the fish throwers at Pike Place Market
description: Trading since 1907, and one of the oldest continuously operating farmers markets in the country. The first Starbucks is across the street.

title: Look for resident orcas in the San Juan Islands
description: The Southern Resident orcas are down to about 73 animals and no longer reliably here - transient Bigg's killer whales are now the more likely sighting.

title: Stand above Palouse Falls
description: A 60m fall into a basalt bowl carved by the Missoula floods at the end of the last ice age. Best in spring melt, and the cliff edges are unfenced.

title: Take the bus into Denali
description: One 148km road into six million acres, and private vehicles are barred beyond mile 15. Grizzly, caribou, moose and wolf all along it.

title: Chase the northern lights from Fairbanks
description: Sitting under the auroral oval, with displays on roughly four nights in five when skies are clear between September and March.

title: Watch tidewater glaciers calve in Kenai Fjords
description: Nearly 40 glaciers flow off the Harding Icefield, several straight into the sea - the boat cuts its engines and you listen to the ice crack.

title: Watch bears fish at Brooks Falls
description: Brown bears catching salmon mid-air from a viewing platform in Katmai. Reachable only by float plane, and the subject of Fat Bear Week.

title: Cruise into Glacier Bay
description: Entirely covered by ice in 1794 and now open water for 100km - one of the fastest documented glacial retreats anywhere. Huna Tlingit homeland.

title: Drive the Dalton Highway to the Arctic Circle
description: 666km of mostly gravel built to service the oil pipeline, with three fuel stops on the entire route and no mobile coverage.

title: Ride the Alaska Railroad to Seward
description: Four hours from Anchorage through country with no road access at all, and one of the last railways anywhere you can flag down from the trackside.

title: Watch Kilauea glow after dark
description: One of the most active volcanoes on earth. Whether there is anything to see depends entirely on the current eruption - check the USGS status first.
